evidence.text: Pictograph of a pestle used for pounding rice, now written as 杵. The current meaning "noon" is a phonetic loan.
啎也。五月，陰气午逆陽。冒地而出。此予矢同意。凡午之屬皆从午。

Pictogram (象形) – a pestle (now written 杵). Unrelated to 干. See the central component of 舂 and 秦 in their original version.
Norman (1985) proposed connection with Austroasiatic; Ferlus (2013) noted a "[g]ood correspondence" between Proto-Vietic *m-ŋəːʔ (whence Vietnamese ngựa) and Old Chinese reconstructions like *m-qʰˁaʔ (Baxter-Sagart) and *ᵀs.ŋaʔ (Ferlus). Also compare Proto-Hlai *hŋaːʔ (“horse”), Proto-Kra *ŋja C (“horse”).
Alternatively, Smith (2011) proposed 午 (OC *ŋaːʔ)'s cognacy with 啎 (OC *ŋaːs) "to meet head on" and 御 (OC *ŋas) "to meet in (battle)" and suggested that "the moon at its full phase opposes the sun directly in the sky, meaning *ŋaaʔ 午 is probably to be glossed, given *-ʔ , ‘facing stage’". Schuessler (2007) regarded 午 (OC ŋâh) "to go against" as a mere graphic variant of 啎 and thus deemed the sense "to go against" distinct from the "earthly branch" sense.

The record identifies 午 as the original graph for 杵 and describes the oracle-bone form as a pestle-shaped club with thick rounded ends and a narrow middle. It describes the upper part of later bronze forms as a corruption of one thick end, then the lower thick end as becoming a horizontal stroke in Chu manuscripts and seal script. It says 午 was later borrowed for an earthly-branch name, after which 杵 was formed with 木 to distinguish the pestle word. The page lists oracle-bone item 合集1718 and bronze item 集成05413. These are source assertions; I did not inspect the glyph images.
evidence.title: 漢字「午」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database likewise analyzes the oracle form as a wooden pounding stick and calls it the early form of 杵. It describes changes from oracle-bone marks to bronze forms and later seal form. As evidence for use as the seventh earthly branch, it cites the bronze inscription 賢簋: 「唯九月初吉庚午」; it also records a bronze personal-name use. It mentions alternative analyses as a horse whip (Luo Zhenyu) or reins (Guo Moruo), but considers the whip analysis unreliable, noting that a separate bronze graph depicts a whip. These are competing graphic interpretations, not established names or pronunciations for the depicted object.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A00431, 說明 and 釋義
evidence.text: The dictionary records the Shuowen explanation 「啎也。五月，陰气午逆陽，冒地而出」, with a variant text in the Duan Yucai edition, and gives modern Mandarin wǔ. Its listed senses include the seventh earthly branch, the time period 11 a.m.–1 p.m., the sun at its daily highest point, crosswise/intersecting, and opposing or contradicting. It cites historical examples for these senses, including Eastern Han branch use and later literary examples for noon. The gloss sequence is not evidence that these senses arose in that order.

evidence.source: Ma Kun, Journal of the Jao Tsung-I Academy of Sinology
evidence.field: “疑紐的上古小舌音來源問題—以「午」、「五」諧聲系列為例”, pp. 225–240
evidence.text: The 2019 paper reports disagreement over the relation and Old Chinese sound of 午 and 五. It presents Baxter–Sagart’s 2014 distinction—午 *[m].qʰˤaʔ versus 五 *C.ŋˤaʔ—and explains that Ho Dah-an instead argued that they were one word with a crosswise sense. The paper sides with keeping their Old Chinese initials distinct. It also reports the common analysis of 午 as the original graph for the pestle word 杵, while noting Ho’s alternative ‘crosswise’ analysis. This debate concerns the 午–五 series; it does not independently establish the original name or pronunciation of the object depicted by 午.
evidence.title: 疑紐的上古小舌音來源問題—以「午」、「五」諧聲系列為例

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The cited paleographic accounts support a pestle interpretation, but I did not inspect the glyph images themselves. The source records identify oracle-bone and bronze exemplars, including 合集1718 and 集成05413, without providing a date for each example in the inspected text.
The CUHK database attests 午 as an earthly branch in a bronze inscription, but the page does not date that vessel. I found no securely dated first use for the branch sense.

The branch-to-noon relationship is reported in the sources, and the Taiwan Ministry dictionary documents the noon and midday-period senses with later textual examples. The exact date and pathway by which 午 acquired the noon sense remain unestablished here; the Shuowen seasonal yin-yang explanation is a historical explanation, not confirmation of that pathway.

For the proposed graph borrowing, the depicted tool is identified by paleographic sources as 杵, but its name and pronunciation at the time of the earliest 午 forms are not independently recovered here. Modern 午 wǔ and 杵 chǔ are distinct; the available inspected sources do not establish the historical phonetic match needed to prove why the graph could be borrowed for the branch word.

The Shuowen page could not be opened, and the direct Unicode Unihan character record was inaccessible. The supplied local row records 午 kMandarin wǔ and local Baxter–Sagart rows give MC nguX with OC *[m].qʰˤaʔ for the branch gloss and *m-qʰˤaʔ for ‘resist; cross-wise’; those rows were checked but are not emitted as external evidence because the corresponding official upstream record could not be verified. No Baxter–Sagart claim about 杵 is made.

The supplied Baxter–Sagart rows are distinct from Zhengzhang’s *ŋaːʔ notation in the dossier. The inspected 2019 study confirms that reconstruction systems and analyses differ; these transcriptions should not be merged or treated as interchangeable.
午 is treated here as a whole graph with pictographic and later borrowed uses, not as a sound component inside a compound. Therefore no component-role account or component sound array is applicable.

No independent historical pronunciation for the depicted pestle name is established in the inspected primary pages. The sources identify the object as a pestle but do not recover its name or sound in the period of the earliest 午 forms; therefore the graph-loan explanation is reported as a source analysis, not independently proven by a sound match.
The CUHK entry cites a bronze inscription with 午 as an earthly-branch sign but does not date the vessel in the inspected text. No securely dated first attestation of branch use is established here.

The Taiwan Ministry dictionary gives later textual examples for midday and the 11 a.m.–1 p.m. period, but this search did not establish the earliest occurrence of the noon sense or a fully documented pathway from the branch name to that time sense. Shuowen’s seasonal yin-yang explanation is a historical account, not independent confirmation of semantic chronology.

The source analyses identify the original graph with 杵, but the depicted implement’s name and pronunciation in the earliest period are not independently established. Current pronunciations or a reconstruction for 午 alone do not prove the proposed graph-loan sound match.

Neither ancient artifact glyph was visually inspected; Sinica and CUHK give paleographic interpretations and catalog identifiers, but do not date the cited exemplars in the opened passages.
